nameStory: The northern brown shrimp gets its name from its brownish coloration and its range along the northern part of the Gulf of Mexico and Atlantic coast. The 'brown' distinguishes it from its close relative, the northern white shrimp, though both can actually show quite a range of colors depending on their environment and diet.
description: Northern brown shrimp are marine crustaceans that belong to the same group as lobsters and crabs, with ten legs (hence 'decapod') and long antennae. They have the classic curved shrimp body shape with a fan-like tail and can grow to about 6-7 inches long. These are the same shrimp you might find on your dinner plate - they're an important commercial species harvested throughout their range. In New England waters, they're quite rare visitors, likely carried north by warm currents.

idTips.label: Body color
idTips.description: Brownish to reddish-brown overall, sometimes with a golden tinge - feels firm and slightly rough when handled fresh

idTips.label: Tail fan
idTips.description: Broad, fan-shaped tail that feels papery thin with distinct grooves you can run your finger along

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Two pairs of long, whip-like antennae that are longer than the body and feel delicate and flexible

idTips.label: Walking legs
idTips.description: Five pairs of jointed legs underneath that feel segmented and articulated when touched

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Large, black compound eyes on stalks that project from the head like little dark marbles

idTips.label: Body texture
idTips.description: Semi-transparent shell that feels smooth but firm, with visible segments you can feel as ridges along the back

habitat: In New England, northern brown shrimp are extremely rare visitors to warmer coastal waters, particularly during summer months when ocean temperatures are highest. They prefer sandy or muddy bottoms in shallow coastal areas and estuaries. Any sightings would likely be in southern New England waters like Buzzards Bay or Narragansett Bay.

seasonality.spring: Extremely unlikely to be seen as waters are still too cool for this warm-water species.
seasonality.summer: Most likely time for rare sightings when ocean temperatures peak and warm currents might carry individuals northward.
seasonality.fall: Possible but unlikely as waters begin cooling, any individuals present would likely move south or perish.
seasonality.winter: Not present - waters are far too cold for survival.

funFact: Northern brown shrimp can actually change color slightly based on their surroundings and diet - those living over dark muddy bottoms tend to be darker brown, while those over lighter sandy areas develop more golden hues, like natural camouflage artists of the seafloor!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with northern white shrimp, but brown shrimp have a distinctly brownish or reddish tinge while white shrimp are more grayish-white. Memory trick: 'Brown shrimp are actually brown, white shrimp are more like gray-white.'
contextualKnowledge: While called 'northern' brown shrimp, they're actually southern species - the 'northern' refers to their position relative to other brown shrimp species found further south in Mexico and Central America. This naming can be confusing since they're essentially tropical visitors to New England waters.
compareHints: Northern brown shrimp are generally more robust and darker than their close relative, the northern white shrimp. Brown shrimp have a more pronounced curve to their body and tend to be slightly larger. The groove along the top of the head (called the rostrum) is also typically shorter and more triangular in brown shrimp compared to the longer, more pointed rostrum of white shrimp.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Northern White Shrimp differs from its close relative, the Northern Brown Shrimp, primarily in coloration - browns have more opaque, brownish-colored shells while whites maintain their characteristic translucent appearance.
